scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that personal goals measure success while arguing they are not the only measure; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: People measure success in very different ways, from wealth and fame to private dreams.
Some people argue that true success can be measured primarily by the goals one sets for oneself.
I agree that personal goals are an important measure of success, but I do not believe they are the only or primary one.
First, measuring success by our own goals is genuinely meaningful.
Each person values different things, so a single standard cannot fairly judge everyone.
For example, someone who dreams of being a caring parent may feel deeply successful without any fame.
This shows that reaching our own goals can bring a real and lasting sense of success.
People who chase only the goals of others often feel empty even when they seem to win.
Setting and meeting personal goals gives our efforts purpose and direction.
To this extent, personal goals are a fair measure of success.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why they are not the only measure

sentences.text: Second, however, success cannot be measured only by the goals we set ourselves.
A person might set very low goals and reach them, yet hardly count as truly successful.
Consider someone whose only goal is to avoid all effort, which she easily achieves by doing nothing.
Such cases show that purely personal goals can be a weak and misleading measure.
Real success often involves the value we create for others, not just for ourselves.
How we affect our family, work, and community also shapes whether a life is truly successful.
Personal goals, then, are one measure of success but far from the only one.
In conclusion, reaching our own goals is a genuine and meaningful form of success.
But success also depends on the value we create and our effect on others.
True success is best measured by both our personal goals and the good we do beyond ourselves.
